name: Gyaru-o (male gyaru)

card.summary: A Japanese street-style for men built on tanned skin, voluminous dyed hair and groomed brows, aimed at a flashy, attention-getting look.
card.note: Artificial tanning carries UV skin risks; the style is high-maintenance.

quick.overview:
Gyaru-o is the male counterpart of Japan's gyaru fashion. It emerged in Shibuya, Tokyo in the late 1990s and is defined by tanned skin, bleached or dyed hair styled up into volume, shaped eyebrows, tight clothing and accessories. The payoff is a deliberately bold, standout appearance.

It peaked in the 2000s, spread through magazines such as Men's Egg, and faded in the 2010s as quieter styles and fast fashion took over. Variants include salon-kei, onii-kei and host-kei, and the broader gyaru scene has seen a revival in recent years.
quick.how: Followers pair a tan (from salons or lotions), lightened and teased hair, and groomed brows with fitted clothes, belts, jewellery and sunglasses. Different substyles shift the look toward biker, host or salon-polished versions.
quick.risks: Tanning beds and UV exposure are linked by dermatologists to skin damage and skin cancer risk, and bleaching hair can dry and weaken it. The look also needs regular upkeep and spending.

lead: Gyaru-o (ギャル男) is a Japanese youth fashion subculture, the male counterpart of gyaru. It is known for tanned skin, high-volume hair, fitted clothing and accessories. [1][2]

It arose in Shibuya in the late 1990s alongside female gyaru, with hair in the voluminous 'sujimori' style and artificial tans central to the look. Men's magazines such as Men's Egg, launched in 1998, spread the style. [1][2]

Popularity peaked in the 2000s and declined in the 2010s, with magazine closures and the rise of cheaper fast fashion often cited. [1] Gyaru culture overall has since been revived in more varied forms. [2]

angle.text: Followers change skin tone, hair colour and shape, and brows to produce a high-impact appearance. The grooming itself is the style.

infobox: Tan, voluminous dyed hair, shaped brows [1]

paras: Hair is lightened or dyed and built up into volume, often with gel, while skin is tanned by salons or products. Eyebrow shaping and accessories such as belts, chains and sunglasses complete the look. [1][2]

Gyaru-o developed in the late 1990s, linked to club culture, para-para dancing and host work, then peaked in the 2000s. [1] It receded in the 2010s as egg magazine ended publication in 2014 and Men's Egg wound down. [1] Wikipedia notes the wider subculture has been revived in the Reiwa era. [2]
